title: Ang 1285–1291: Malar ki Var ends
tomorrow: a singer gets thrown out of a temple. what does the temple do?

lines: THE CERTIFICATES ARE THE HARD PART.
cards: Saturday, and Simran's bedroom floor is three piles: keep, give away, and a trash bag. The certificates are the hard part. A spelling bee ribbon, a science fair medal, the honor roll her dad framed.
Nobody looks at those in a dorm room. Near the end of Guru Nanak's rain ballad there's a line about exactly this kind of pile, and it doesn't say keep.

teach.b: The ballad's second half begins on ang 1285, and close to its end, on ang 1290, comes the line.

teach.h: NOT THE PEOPLE. NOT THE WORK.
teach.b: In paraphrase: Nanak says, burn the world's praises in the fire; they made people forget the Name. Not the people who gave them. Not the work behind them.
The praise, when it crowds out what matters.
That's where the rain ballad is heading as it closes. Now hold up the week. A key, given, that opens the mind's locked room.
A test in the hands: earn, eat, give. Four bhagats, and the company you keep. Malar, and rain on a dry field.
Birha, missing someone as a kind of love. One storm, glad for some, hard for others. And now, praise that can make you forget.
Simran keeps one ribbon, the one Bebe pinned on her.
The frame goes to her dad's office, where he'll actually see it. The rest goes in the bag. She doesn't burn a thing.
The line was never about matches.

how: Malar ki Var is sung in kirtan pauri by pauri with its saloks; readers find its second half from ang 1285, ending before the bhagats' hymns in Malar.

s: the line on ang 1290 tells you to set your awards on fire
it burns the praise that makes people forget the Name, not people, work or ribbons.
both of this week's ballads set saloks before their pauris
Sarang ki Var and Malar ki Var: stanzas, with short verses before them.

games.q: a friend's post about her award gets lots of likes, and she refreshes it all night. which line from this week fits best?
o: the world's praise can crowd out what matters.
earn, eat, give: she earned it, so enjoy all of it.
rain on the just and unjust: everyone gets likes.
games.why: near the end of the rain ballad, Guru Nanak says to burn the world's praise in the fire, because it made people forget the Name.

practice: Find one thing near you that holds praise of you: a certificate, a medal, a kind message saved on your phone. Hold it, or just bring it to mind, and breathe slowly.
Ask it quietly what it helps you remember, and what it might help you forget.

wordCard.voice: Ang 1285. Where the rain ballad's second half begins, on its way to a line about the world's praise and the fire.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: vadiaaee, greatness or praise; the salok speaks of the world's praises.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: the ballad ends by asking what your praise makes you forget. A week of ballads and rain, done.
